title: What Clone Really Costs
goal: Clone always compiles. This deck is about when it is the wrong tool.

sections.text: Calling `.clone()` on a `String` or a `Vec` allocates new heap memory and copies every element. The program stays correct, so the compiler never warns you. That is what makes clone dangerous: it is the easy way past a borrow-checker error, and it silently costs an allocation each time.

sections.caption: Clone-then-borrow is the most common clone smell.

sections.text: A clone is justified in exactly one case: both sides need ownership of the data at the same time. If the function only reads, a borrow does the job. If the caller never uses the value again, a move does the job. A clone inside a loop deserves extra suspicion, because its cost multiplies by the iteration count.

For small plain-data types there is a third option. A struct that holds only fixed-size fields, like two `i32` values, can derive `Copy`. Then passing it duplicates it automatically, and every `.clone()` on it becomes noise. Clippy flags that case with the clone_on_copy lint.
Each puzzle in this deck starts with code that clones too much. Your job is to find which clones a borrow, a move, or a derive can replace.

explanation: Clone only when both sides need ownership. A borrow, a move, or a Copy derive removes most clones.
